report:
Your skepticism is understandable, but the specific claim is **supported for incidence reduction**, with important caveats. In the randomized NCIC CTG MAP.3 trial, 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk received exemestane 25 mg/day or placebo; at ~35 months median follow-up, invasive breast cancer was reduced by about 65% (HR 0.35), with adverse events 88% vs 85% and no significant fracture/cardiovascular difference at that point (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507). ASCO’s guideline says clinicians should discuss aromatase inhibitors, including exemestane, for risk reduction in postmenopausal women at increased risk, while avoiding them in premenopausal women (https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.19.01472). USPSTF similarly supports offering risk-reducing medication to women at increased risk and low risk of medication harms, though it emphasizes individualized benefit–harm assessment (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction).

The defensible “false” version would be narrower: exemestane has **not been shown to reduce breast-cancer mortality or overall mortality** in prevention, absolute benefit is modest, and harms matter—hot flashes, arthralgia, and bone-density loss/fracture risk require monitoring (https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20151012/exemestane-negatively-affects-bone-health-in-postmenopausal-women). Bottom line: the claim is true as an **incidence-reduction** statement in elevated-risk postmenopausal women; it is overstated if read as proven survival benefit or risk-free prevention.
